title: GraphQL Resolvers: The Chain, The Args, The Execution
summary: A deep field-by-field tour of how GraphQL resolvers actually run: the four arguments, the parent-to-child resolver chain, default resolvers, execution order and concurrency, context and dataloaders, errors and nullability, and the performance traps that bite real schemas.

chapters.title: What A Resolver Actually Is
points: Definition: a resolver is a function attached to one field of one type that returns the value for that field
Signature in graphql-js: resolve(parent, args, context, info) — four positional arguments, always in that order
Resolvers live in a resolver map keyed by type name then field name: { Query: { user: fn }, User: { posts: fn } }
A resolver resolves a FIELD, not a type — 'User resolver' is loose talk for 'resolvers on User's fields'
The schema (SDL) declares shape and types; resolvers supply behavior — they are two separate layers glued at makeExecutableSchema/buildSchema time
Query, Mutation, Subscription are ordinary object types; their fields are the entry points, nothing more special
Example: const resolvers = { Query: { hello: () => 'world' } } with type Query { hello: String }
A resolver may return a scalar, object, array, null, a Promise, or throw — the executor handles all five
Returning a Promise is normal; the executor awaits it before descending into child fields
Resolvers are not middleware and not controllers: one field, one job, called once per parent object per request
Field arguments declared in SDL (user(id: ID!)) arrive in the args object, already coerced and validated
Leaf fields (scalars, enums) end the chain — after their resolver returns, serialization happens and no children are visited
Mental model: GraphQL execution is a depth-first walk of the query AST where each node calls one resolver
Gotcha: a field with no resolver is not an error — the default resolver quietly takes over (see the defaults chapter)

chapters.title: The Four Arguments: parent, args, context, info
points: parent (a.k.a. root, source, obj): the value returned by the resolver of the PARENT field — this is the whole resolver chain in one argument
For top-level Query fields, parent is the rootValue passed to graphql()/execute(), usually undefined or {}
args: an object of the field's arguments, already type-coerced, defaults applied, and nulls distinguished from absent keys
args only contains arguments declared on THAT field in the SDL — undeclared arguments fail validation before execution
context: one object created per request, shared by every resolver in that request — the place for db clients, the authed user, dataloaders, request headers
context is built by the server integration (Apollo's context function, Yoga's context) and must never be a module-level global
info: the resolver's view of execution — fieldName, fieldNodes, returnType, parentType, path, schema, fragments, operation, variableValues, rootValue
info.path is a linked list of the exact traversal position, e.g. user > posts > 2 > title — best thing to log in errors
info.fieldNodes lets you inspect the sub-selection to do projection (only SELECT the columns actually requested)
Rule of thumb: read from parent, filter with args, get resources from context, and touch info only for optimization or logging
Example: posts: (user, { first = 10 }, { db }) => db.posts.byAuthor(user.id, first)
Argument order is positional — a resolver written (args, context) is silently wrong because args lands in the parent slot
Arrow functions vs. method shorthand: 'this' is not meaningful inside resolvers; never rely on it
Anti-pattern: stuffing per-field state onto context to pass data sideways between sibling resolvers — execution order makes that unreliable
Gotcha: mutating the parent object inside a child resolver leaks across sibling fields sharing that same object reference

chapters.title: The Resolver Chain: Parent Feeds Child
points: The chain rule: whatever a field's resolver returns becomes the `parent` argument of every resolver on that field's sub-selection
Worked example: Query.user returns { id: 7, name: 'Ada' } → User.posts receives that exact object as parent
The returned object need not match the GraphQL type's shape — it only needs enough data for the child resolvers to do their work
Common pattern: return a thin row from the database ({ id, author_id }) and let child resolvers hydrate the rest lazily
Chain depth equals query depth: a 4-level query runs 4 layers of resolvers, each layer fanning out over the previous layer's results
List fields fan out: if Query.users returns 20 users, User.name runs 20 times — once per item, with parent set to that item
Nested lists multiply: 20 users × 10 posts each = 200 calls to Post.title — this is the N+1 shape in its native habitat
Null short-circuits the branch: if a resolver returns null, its child resolvers are never called for that branch
Returning a Promise of a list is fine; returning a list of Promises is also fine — the executor awaits each item
The chain crosses type boundaries: Post.author returning a user id means User.name's parent is whatever Post.author resolved to, not the original user
Circular queries (user → posts → author → posts) are legal and just keep walking the chain — depth-limit them in production
Passing data down the chain deliberately: return { ...row, _tenantId } and read it in the child, instead of re-fetching
Trade-off: fat parents (fetch everything up front, few resolvers) vs. thin parents (fetch per field, more round-trips but no over-fetching)
Gotcha: a child resolver that assumes a hydrated parent breaks the moment another query path reaches that type with a thin parent

chapters.title: Default Resolvers: The Invisible Majority
points: If a field has no resolver in the map, graphql-js calls defaultFieldResolver instead — most fields in a real schema use it
defaultFieldResolver(source, args, ctx, info): reads source[info.fieldName]; if that value is a function it CALLS it with (args, ctx, info) and returns the result
So a plain object { name: 'Ada' } resolves User.name for free — no resolver needed
Class instances work too: a getter or method named `name` on the parent instance is invoked by the default resolver
The function-calling branch is why ORM model methods sometimes 'just work' as GraphQL fields — and why they get called with args as the first parameter
Undefined property → the field resolves to null (or errors if the field is non-null)
Property name must match the field name exactly — snake_case columns vs. camelCase fields is the single most common 'why is it null' bug
Fix options for name mismatch: alias in SQL, map in the model layer, write an explicit one-line resolver, or use a field-name-mapping directive
You can override defaults globally: pass fieldResolver to execute(), or set defaultFieldResolver via schema transforms/plugins
Explicit resolvers always win over the default for that field
Performance: the default resolver is a property read — vastly cheaper than a user-written resolver that hits a service; don't add resolvers you don't need
Type resolvers are different: interfaces and unions need __resolveType (or isTypeOf on each member) — there is no useful default
Default __resolveType behavior: graphql-js falls back to source.__typename if present, otherwise errors 'Abstract type must resolve to an Object type'
Scalar leaf values still go through the scalar's serialize() after the default resolver returns them
Gotcha: a Date object resolving into a String field silently becomes an ISO string via String coercion — declare a custom scalar instead

chapters.title: Execution Order and Concurrency
points: Execution is breadth-per-level, depth-overall: all fields of one selection set start, then each result is descended into
Query fields execute in PARALLEL — the spec permits any order and graphql-js kicks them all off then awaits
Mutation top-level fields execute SERIALLY, in the order written in the document — this is the one ordering guarantee in the spec
Serial mutations only apply to the ROOT mutation fields; everything nested under them is parallel again
Practical consequence: two mutations in one document run one-after-another, so a create followed by a read in the same document sees the write
Sibling fields at the same level must be treated as order-independent — never let one sibling depend on another's side effect
Field collection happens first: fragments are flattened and identically-aliased fields merged before any resolver runs
Same field requested twice with the same arguments is executed once (merged); with different arguments and different aliases it runs twice
The executor awaits every Promise at a level before moving to the next level of the tree
@skip / @include are evaluated during field collection, so excluded fields never call a resolver at all
Response key order follows query order, even though resolution order does not — the serialized JSON is deterministic
graphql-js's ExecuteField loop: resolve value → complete value (unwrap non-null, iterate lists, recurse into objects, serialize leaves)
@defer / @stream (incremental delivery) break the single-response assumption: parts of the tree resolve after the initial payload
Subscriptions run once per published event: the source stream yields a value, then normal parallel execution runs over that payload
Gotcha: relying on 'resolvers run top to bottom' to sequence writes is a bug that only appears under load

chapters.title: Context, Auth, and Per-Request State
points: Context is created once per request, before execution, and passed unchanged to every resolver in the tree
Typical contents: authenticated user/claims, database or ORM handle, dataloaders, request-scoped logger, trace id, feature flags
Never put per-field or mutable cross-resolver state in context — parallel execution makes ordering assumptions false
Dataloaders MUST be created per request inside the context factory; a module-level dataloader leaks cached data between users
Auth in resolvers: check context.user at the field where the data is exposed, not only at the entry point — nested paths reach the same type
Field-level authorization pattern: a wrapper/higher-order resolver, e.g. requireRole('admin')(resolverFn)
Schema-directive authorization (@auth(requires: ADMIN)) wraps defaultFieldResolver via a schema transform so unresolved fields are covered too
Auth errors should be thrown, not returned as null, so the client sees an errors entry with a code extension
Context typing in TypeScript: define one Context interface and parameterize the generated resolver types so every resolver is checked
Batching/transaction handle on context lets a mutation run all its writes in one database transaction
Subscriptions get context per connection (and often per event) — connection auth differs from HTTP request auth
Cost tracking and depth limiting typically read info + context together in a validation rule or plugin, not inside resolvers
Testing: build a fake context object and call the resolver function directly — no HTTP server needed
Gotcha: caching a fetch result on context for the whole request is fine; caching it in module scope is a cross-tenant data leak

chapters.title: N+1, DataLoader, and Resolver Performance
points: N+1 defined: one query for the list plus one query per item because the child resolver fetches individually
Concrete cost: 50 posts each calling Post.author → 1 + 50 database round trips instead of 2
DataLoader fixes it by batching: collect all .load(key) calls in one tick, then call your batchFn(keys) once
batchFn contract: given keys [1,2,3] you must return values in the SAME order and SAME length, with null/Error for misses
DataLoader also memoizes per instance, so the same key requested by 10 resolvers hits the database once
Batching window is the microtask tick — resolvers running in the same execution level get batched together naturally
Per-request instantiation is mandatory: cache lifetime = request lifetime, or you serve stale/foreign data
Alternative to per-field loading: join up front in the parent resolver and let default resolvers read the already-joined fields
Look-ahead optimization: read info.fieldNodes to build a projection/JOIN only for the fields actually requested
Query cost analysis and depth limits (graphql-depth-limit, cost directives) protect against pathological nesting before execution starts
Resolver-level caching: cache by (parentId, args) in a request cache; cross-request caching needs explicit invalidation and auth-aware keys
Trade-off table: DataLoader (low code change, still N queries batched into 1 per level) vs. eager JOIN (1 query, over-fetches) vs. per-field fetch (simple, slowest)
Measure with tracing: Apollo tracing / OpenTelemetry gives per-resolver duration keyed by info.path
Async overhead is real: thousands of tiny async resolvers cost measurable time — returning plain values instead of Promises where possible helps
Gotcha: DataLoader hides the N+1 in your metrics dashboard but not in your database if your batchFn itself loops

chapters.title: Errors, Nullability, and Return Shapes
points: A thrown error becomes an entry in the response's `errors` array, with message, locations, and path from info.path
Nullable field that errors → that field becomes null, siblings still resolve, execution continues
Non-null field (String!) that errors or returns null → the error propagates UP to the nearest nullable ancestor, nulling that whole subtree
Worst case: an errored non-null field under a non-null chain nulls `data` entirely — one bad row kills the response
Design rule: make fields nullable by default; reserve ! for values that genuinely cannot be absent
[Post!]! vs [Post]! vs [Post]: the inner ! nulls the whole list if one element fails; no inner ! nulls only that element
Return null vs. throw: null means 'no value', throw means 'something went wrong' — 'not found' is a design choice, pick one and be consistent
Expected errors as data: union/result types (type UserResult = User | NotFoundError) keep failures typed and in `data`
Error extensions carry machine-readable codes (extensions.code = 'FORBIDDEN'), plus stacktrace in dev only
formatError/maskedErrors hooks strip internal messages before they reach clients — never leak SQL or stack traces in production
Unhandled Promise rejections inside a resolver are caught by the executor; unhandled rejections in fire-and-forget side calls are not
Resolvers should not return the raw GraphQL type name — __typename is derived from the schema or __resolveType, not from your return value's shape
Partial success is normal in GraphQL: clients must be written to handle data + errors together, unlike REST's single status code
Gotcha: catching every error and returning null makes debugging impossible — log with info.path before swallowing

chapters.title: Beyond Object Fields: Interfaces, Unions, Subscriptions, Directives
points: __resolveType(value, context, info) picks the concrete object type for an interface or union; return a type name string
isTypeOf(value, context, info) is the per-member alternative: each object type answers 'is this mine?'; slower because it may be probed in order
Once the concrete type is chosen, that type's field resolvers run normally — abstract types add one step, not a new mechanism
Adding __typename in the parent's returned row is the cheapest __resolveType strategy
Subscriptions have TWO functions per field: subscribe() returns an AsyncIterator, resolve() maps each published payload to the field value
Without an explicit subscription resolve(), the default resolver reads payload[fieldName] — a classic source of null subscription events
withFilter / async generator filtering decides which published events reach which subscriber, using args and context
Schema directives are implemented as resolver wrappers: a mapSchema transform replaces field.resolve with a function calling the original (or defaultFieldResolver)
Wrapping order matters when several directives apply to the same field — the outermost wrapper runs first
Custom scalars are not resolvers: serialize (out), parseValue (variable in), parseLiteral (inline in) — three functions on GraphQLScalarType
Enum values may have internal values that differ from the SDL name; resolvers return the internal value
Federation adds __resolveReference(reference, context, info) so a subgraph can resolve an entity from just its key fields
Federation @external/@requires/@provides change which fields a subgraph's resolvers must supply — the chain now spans services
Gotcha: interfaces implemented by types across files need the type map registered, or __resolveType returns a name that isn't in the schema

chapters.title: Mistakes, Trade-offs, and the One-Page Recap
points: Recap of the signature: (parent, args, context, info) — parent is the chain, args is the query, context is the request, info is the position
Recap of order: Query fields parallel, root Mutation fields serial, everything nested parallel, field collection before any of it
Recap of defaults: no resolver → read parent[fieldName], call it if it's a function — this covers most of a real schema
Mistake: wrong argument position — writing (args, context) and reading undefined properties
Mistake: snake_case database columns against camelCase schema fields, producing silent nulls via the default resolver
Mistake: creating DataLoader outside the request, leaking one user's data to another
Mistake: depending on sibling resolver order or on side effects set by another field
Mistake: over-using ! so a single failing field nulls the whole response
Mistake: business logic inside resolvers instead of a service layer — resolvers should be thin adapters that are trivially testable
Mistake: fetching in the parent AND re-fetching in the child, doubling the load for no benefit
Trade-off: thin parent + per-field resolvers (composable, N+1-prone) vs. fat parent + default resolvers (fast, over-fetches, couples types)
Trade-off: DataLoader everywhere (uniform, adds indirection) vs. targeted JOINs (fastest for known hot paths, more code)
Trade-off: errors as thrown exceptions (simple, partial nulls) vs. result unions (typed, verbose schema)
Checklist before shipping a resolver: correct arg order, per-request context deps, batched fetch, nullability chosen deliberately, error logged with info.path, no cross-sibling state
Debug drill: log info.path + info.fieldName + typeof parent at the top of a suspect resolver — it answers 'why null' faster than anything else

Final mental model: a GraphQL response is a tree built by one function call per field per parent, and every performance and correctness question reduces to how many of those calls run and what each one touches
